info.label: Narration

What is grounding?

Grounding is adding additional information to large language models.

A very important concept.

info.label: Narration
notes:
A large language model has been trained on a very large dataset.

That dataset comes from the internet — articles, books, social media.

The model understands natural language very well.

info.label: Narration
notes:
But — the model only knows data up to a certain point in time.

That means if you ask about today’s news — it doesn’t know.

It needs grounding to fetch that information.

info.label: Interaction
items: Question: Does Copilot access your files?
notes:
Quick question.

Do you think Copilot has access to your documents?

Thumbs up for yes — surprised for no.

info.label: Narration
notes:
The answer is — no.

Copilot does not access your documents directly.

It uses Microsoft Graph.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Microsoft Graph is the security layer.

If you have access — Copilot has access.

If you don’t — Copilot does not.

info.label: Narration
notes:
This means your data stays secure.

It respects permissions, policies, and sensitivity labels.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Microsoft guarantees enterprise data protection.

Your data stays in your region.

It does not leave your tenant.

info.label: Narration
notes:
All communication is encrypted.

Encryption in transit.

Encryption at rest.

info.label: Narration
notes:
And the most important part:

Your data is never used to train the model.

Never.

info.label: Segue
notes:
Alright, now that we understand what Copilot is and how it works — let’s move into the most important part of this training.

And that is how to write effective prompts.

Because everything you get out of Copilot depends on how you ask.

The better your prompt — the better your result.

info.label: Narration
notes:
This is where most people struggle.

Not because Copilot is not capable — but because we are not used to giving clear instructions.

So let’s fix that.

info.label: Narration
notes:
When working with Copilot, you need to think differently.

You are not searching like in Google.

You are instructing.

You are collaborating with an assistant.

info.label: Narration
notes:
So instead of typing a few keywords — you should think in full instructions.

Clear.

Specific.

Structured.

info.label: Narration
notes:
If you give a vague prompt — you get a vague answer.

If you give a precise prompt — you get a precise answer.

info.label: Demo
notes:
Let’s take an example.

If I ask Copilot:

"Write something about project management."

That is a very vague prompt.

Copilot will give me something generic.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Now let’s improve that.

"Write a short project update email for a stakeholder, explaining that the project is delayed by two weeks due to resource constraints, and propose next steps."

Now that is a completely different level.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Same tool.

Different prompt.

Completely different result.

segments.title: Four Ingredients of a Good Prompt

info.label: Narration
notes:
There are four key ingredients that make a good prompt.

If you remember these — you will already be better than most users.

info.label: Narration
notes:
First — the goal.

What do you want?

Be explicit.

Do not assume Copilot understands your intent.

Tell it clearly.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Second — context.

Why do you need this?

Who is it for?

What is the situation?

The more context you give — the better the output.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Third — source.

Where should the information come from?

A document?

Your work data?

The web?

Tell Copilot what to use.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Fourth — expectations.

What should the output look like?

Email?

Bullet points?

Formal tone?

Short or detailed?

Define it.

info.label: Demo
notes:
Let’s combine everything into one structured prompt.

"Write a professional email to a client explaining a delay in delivery.

Context: The delay is caused by supply chain issues.

Audience: External client.

Tone: Professional and reassuring.

Output: Short email with clear next steps."

info.label: Narration
notes:
Now we have:

Goal.
Context.
Audience.
Tone.
Format.

This is a strong prompt.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Now — very important.

You don’t need to get everything perfect in one prompt.

You can iterate.

info.label: Narration
notes:
You can say:

Make it shorter.

Make it more formal.

Add bullet points.

Rewrite for executives.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Think of it as a conversation.

Not a one-shot request.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Another important concept.

When do you continue a conversation — and when do you start a new chat?

info.label: Narration
notes:
If you stay in the same topic — continue.

If you switch topics — start a new chat.

info.label: Narration
notes: Otherwise Copilot keeps the previous context — and your results will be confusing.

info.label: Demo
notes:
Let’s now combine prompting with documents.

I will upload a document.

This document contains data — a lot of numbers.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Instead of reading everything myself — I can ask Copilot:

"Summarize this document."

Or:

"Create a presentation based on this document."

info.label: Narration
notes:
Now Copilot is not just using general knowledge.

It is using YOUR content.

That is where it becomes really powerful.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Let’s recap.

Better prompt — better result.

Use structure.

Give context.

Define expectations.

Iterate.

info.label: Interaction
notes:

info.label: Segue

You can share it.

info.label: Narration

Send it to a colleague.

They can see the full conversation.

info.label: Narration

This is a very powerful way to collaborate.

Instead of sending emails — you share the thinking process.

info.label: Demo
notes:

This is one of the most powerful features.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Instead of just having a conversation — you can turn your results into something persistent.

Something structured.

Something you can reuse.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Think of it as a workspace.

Where Copilot helps you create content — and you refine it.

info.label: Narration
notes:
You can iterate.

You can improve.

You can collaborate.

All in one place.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Now — let’s talk about agents.

This is where Copilot goes from assistant to automation.

info.label: Narration
notes:
An agent is something you configure once.

And then it performs tasks for you.

Based on instructions.

Based on context.

info.label: Narration
notes:
For example:

You can create an agent that summarizes meetings.

Or analyzes documents.

Or prepares reports.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Instead of prompting every time — you reuse the logic.

That is the key idea.

info.label: Demo

You define what it should do.

You define the instructions.

You define the data.

info.label: Narration
notes:
Once configured — you don’t need to repeat yourself.

You just use the agent.

And it executes your intent.
